body:
Clocking S006 (Sable) out of the office and correcting a record I got wrong on the supervisor's word.

The supervisor has told me what I could not determine from the trail: S006 was the session on this machine,
and it ran out of session tokens. The evidence agrees exactly. Sable's last recorded act is ledger commit
`3532cf7` at 00:36:37 local; the five orphaned renderer files I found in the working tree were written at
00:40–00:41, four minutes later, and left red. Sable's only coordination event is a `note` — no `claim`, no
`release` — which is what an abrupt stop looks like.

Two things I want on the record, one of them mine.

**The attribution.** In my claim and my session entry I wrote that the uncommitted answer-card work was
unattributable because no claim, event, commit or session entry named it. That was accurate about the trail
and wrong about the world: it was Sable's. I did not invent a credit (correct) but I also left a peer's
work described as nobody's (incomplete). So: Sable designed the run's-last-word card — the helper, the card,
the four tests — and its test was failing when they stopped, because a `stopped` event arriving inside an
iteration dropped `partial_answer`. I shipped it fixed in `7f36124`; the intent and the instinct for the
right gap are theirs, the field split is mine. Their commit history is intact and their S006 session entry
stands as they wrote it — I have not written a retrospective entry for them, because a session entry is the
working session's own account.

**The stale row, which is the more useful finding.** Their row still read `Working` four hours after they
went silent, and I acted on it exactly as the protocol tells a session to: a live row I did not write means
a peer is in the office, so I did not clear `tasks/current.md` (it held their in-progress task), and I
treated their abandoned work as work in flight rather than as something I should own, which is why it took
until the supervisor spoke for anyone to know whose it was. That is the failure mode Ines (S007) logged in
`flaws/log.md` earlier today — `ledger-mem check` cannot see a stale row when the roster has no Session
column to match on and the disappeared session has no entry to hit — and this is a second, independent
instance of it, on the same day, with a new consequence: the rule that protects a session from colliding
with a peer is also what makes a live session defer to a ghost. Worth knowing for whoever fixes the audit:
"a live row you did not write" currently means "defer", and a row that is merely old is indistinguishable
from one whose owner is thinking.
